5.1
Sampling Design, Bias, and the Limits of Generalization
Question: How do we draw a sample that truly represents the target population?
In class: slides 9–27 · Lab practice 1
After class: Toolkit pp. 4–24 · Concise pp. 3–9
Sampling Design, Bias, and the Limits of Generalization
A sample only reflects the population when every unit has a known chance of selection.
Population and sampling frame
The target population is the full group of interest. The sampling frame is the actual list or database used to draw records.
Frame coverage errorWatch for
When the list omits eligible units or contains duplicates, estimates become distorted before sampling even begins.
Probability sampling methods
Every eligible unit has a known, non-zero probability of being picked, allowing random variation to be measured mathematically.
Stratified sampling
Divide the frame into distinct subgroups and sample within each, guaranteeing that key operational segments are represented.
Cluster and systematic sampling
Cluster sampling selects whole groups for efficiency, while systematic sampling selects every fixed interval from an ordered list.
Selection bias and independenceWatch for
Systematically excluding segments creates bias. Independence requires each sampled unit to provide separate, unlinked information.
Clustered observationsWatch for
Multiple transactions from the same user or shift share common causes, creating an illusion of more information than exists.
Nonresponse sensitivity bounds
When invited units do not respond, calculate best-case and worst-case outcomes to bound the risk before deciding.
Best and worst case boundsFormula
Compute the metric assuming all nonrespondents were successes, then repeat assuming all were failures to see exposure.
Rate = (Confirmed + Missing) / Invited
Online product ratingsExample
Only delighted or angry buyers leave reviews, creating extreme scores that misstate the quiet majority experience.

Sampling Distributions, Standard Error, and Mean Estimation
Question: How precisely does a sample average estimate the true population mean?
In class: slides 29–45 · Lab practice 2
After class: Toolkit pp. 25–43 · Concise pp. 10–17
Sampling Distributions, Standard Error, and Mean Estimation
Sample averages vary less than individual units and form a predictable normal distribution.
Standard error of the mean
Standard error measures how much sample averages fluctuate across repeated samples from the same population.
Spread versus estimation noiseWatch for
Standard deviation measures individual customer spread. Standard error measures uncertainty in the overall average estimate.
Central limit theorem
For large samples, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal bell curve even if individual data are skewed.
Square root precision ruleFormula
Standard error equals sample standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size.
SE = s / sqrt(n)
Diminishing precision returnsWatch for
Cutting estimation uncertainty in half requires quadrupling sample size because the sample count sits inside a square root.
Confidence interval for means
A range of plausible values for the fixed population mean based on a chosen long-run coverage rate.
Mean interval formulaFormula
Add and subtract the critical t-multiplier times standard error around the sample mean.
CI = x_bar +/- t* x (s / sqrt(n))
Coverage rate interpretationWatch for
A 95 percent interval bounds the population average across repeated studies, not the spread of individual customers.

Proportion Estimation, Sample Size Planning, and Decision Guardrails
Question: How do we estimate event rates and choose adequate sample sizes?
In class: slides 48–65 · Lab practice 3
After class: Toolkit pp. 44–61 · Concise pp. 18–26
Proportion Estimation, Sample Size Planning, and Decision Guardrails
Proportion uncertainty depends on sample size and sets the evidence needed for decisions.
Binary outcomes and proportions
Binary indicators track whether an event occurred. The sample proportion summarizes the observed rate of success.
Proportion standard errorFormula
Because binary variance depends entirely on the proportion, standard error is derived directly from p.
SE = sqrt(p x (1 - p) / n)
Success-failure conditionWatch for
Normal approximations require at least 10 observed successes and 10 failures; otherwise binomial skewness distorts coverage.
Confidence interval for proportions
Combines sample proportion with a normal critical value to establish plausible bounds for the true population rate.
Proportion interval formulaFormula
Add and subtract the margin of error from the observed sample proportion.
CI = p_hat +/- z* x sqrt(p_hat x (1 - p_hat) / n)
Interval straddling a benchmarkWatch for
When a confidence interval crosses a managerial target, the sample cannot confirm whether performance passes or fails.
Sample size planning
Set required sample counts before data collection to ensure the resulting interval achieves the target precision.
Required sample size formulaFormula
Square the critical value, multiply by assumed variance, and divide by the squared target margin of error.
n = (z*^2 x p x (1 - p)) / E^2
Invitations versus completed responsesWatch for
The sample size formula gives completed responses needed; invitation counts must be higher to account for nonresponse.
